title: Surface Areas and Volumes
prerequisites: Surface area and volume formulae for cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere.
Value of π and skill with fractions.
Pythagoras theorem for finding slant height.

topics.title: Combination of Solids
topics.quick_summary: For a solid made by joining two shapes, volumes always add, but only the exposed surfaces are counted in the surface area.
topics.real_life: A capsule is a cylinder with a hemisphere at each end, and a circus tent is a cylinder topped by a cone — both standard combination problems.

detailed.definition: A combination of solids is formed by joining two or more standard solids, or by removing one from another. Its volume is the sum or difference of the component volumes.
detailed.key_idea: Surfaces that are joined together disappear from view and must not be counted. Volumes, by contrast, always add without exception — this asymmetry is the heart of the chapter.
detailed.working_principle: Identify the component solids, decide which faces remain exposed, add only those areas, and add all the volumes.
applications: Cylinder + hemisphere: total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr² + πr² (base), if the base is exposed.
Cone on a cylinder (a tent): canvas needed = curved surface of cone + curved surface of cylinder.
A cylinder with a conical cavity: subtract the cone's volume but add its curved surface.

points: Volumes always add; only exposed surface areas add.
The circular faces where two solids join are not part of the surface area.
Draw the solid and mark which faces are visible before writing any formula.
For a cone, the curved surface uses slant height l = √(r² + h²).
Check that r is the same for both parts where they join.
mistakes: Including the joined circular faces in the total surface area.
Using the vertical height instead of the slant height for a cone's curved surface.
Subtracting volumes when the solids are joined rather than hollowed out.
topics.memory_hook: 'Add all volumes, but only the surfaces you can actually see.'
topics.advanced: For a hollowed solid the surface area may increase even though the volume decreases, because a new internal surface is created. Volume and surface area are genuinely independent quantities.

topics.title: Conversion of Solids and Frustum of a Cone
topics.quick_summary: When a solid is melted and recast the volume stays constant, and a frustum is the part of a cone left after cutting off the top parallel to the base.
topics.real_life: A bucket, a lampshade and a drinking glass are all frustums, and melting a metal sphere into wire is a volume-conservation problem.

detailed.definition: A frustum of a cone is the solid remaining when a cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base and the upper cone is removed. Its slant height is l = √[h² + (R − r)²].
detailed.key_idea: In every melting, recasting or reshaping problem the volume is conserved while the surface area changes freely. Setting the two volumes equal is always the first line of the solution.
detailed.working_principle: The frustum formulas come from subtracting the small cone from the large one; the algebra is done once and the result quoted.
applications: Number of small articles from a large one = volume of large ÷ volume of one small.
A bucket's capacity is a frustum volume; the metal sheet needed is its curved surface plus the base.
Water flowing through a pipe: volume = cross-sectional area × speed × time.

points: In melting and recasting, volume is conserved but surface area is not.
Frustum curved surface = πl(R + r), with l = √[h² + (R − r)²].
Frustum total surface = πl(R + r) + πR² + πr².
For a flowing pipe, volume delivered = area of cross-section × flow speed × time.
mistakes: Using l = √(h² + R² + r²) instead of √[h² + (R − r)²].
Equating surface areas instead of volumes in a recasting problem.
Forgetting that a bucket usually has no lid, so the top circle is not included.
topics.memory_hook: 'Melt and recast: volume never changes' — and for a frustum, use (R − r) in the slant height.
topics.advanced: Letting r → 0 turns the frustum formula into the cone formula, and r → R turns it into the cylinder formula. A single expression contains both as limiting cases.

formulas.name: Frustum of a Cone
formulas.formula: V = (1/3)πh(R² + r² + Rr);  CSA = πl(R + r);  l = √[h² + (R − r)²]
formulas.variables: R = larger radius, r = smaller radius, h = vertical height, l = slant height.
formulas.when_to_use: For buckets, glasses, lampshades and any truncated cone.
formulas.common_mistakes: Adding R and r inside the slant-height root instead of subtracting.
formulas.shortcut: Setting r = 0 recovers the cone formulas as a check.
